scribe_response.text: What do you remember about your school days? My school was a long low building of whitewashed brick, about a mile from our house. We called it the Board School, and it stood beside a banyan tree that older boys were forbidden to climb. Every morning we sat on benches in rows, and the headmaster walked down the aisle with his hands uh behind his back. His name was Mister Pillai, and he had a voice like a slow drum. We began each day with a prayer and then recited the multiplication tables up to twenty. I can still repeat them in the same singsong rhythm, and sometimes they help me fall asleep. We wrote on slates until the um fifth class. The chalk dust settled on our fingers like flour. When we finally received notebooks, I treated mine as if it were made of gold leaf. My handwriting was neat because my father had trained me to hold the pen lightly. Mathematics was my favourite subject, and I loved geometry above all the other branches. I liked the idea that a drawing could prove something, that um a circle and a ruler could settle um an argument. Our geometry teacher was a thin man with a limp, and he drew perfect circles freehand on the blackboard. Once I asked him how he managed it, and he said that he simply stopped worrying. What happened next? I thought about that sentence for years, and I now think it was good advice for engineers. Our English lessons were taught from a worn reader printed in London, full of snowy villages. We had never seen snow, so we imagined it as a kind of cold white rice. Still, I enjoyed uh the stories, and I read them aloud to my sister Meena at night. Science classes were held on Fridays, and uh the teacher brought a magnet and a glass jar of mercury. He let us watch the silver drops roll across a tray, and nobody dared to breathe. I was lucky to have a father who was himself a teacher, though he worked at another school across the river. He never helped me in class and never boasted about my marks. Instead he corrected my spelling at home, patiently, with his red pencil. At the end of the year there was a prize day in the courtyard, with plastic chairs and a rented microphone. I received the prize for mathematics three times. Each time my mother wrapped the book in brown paper. The other boys did not hold it against me, because I let them copy my homework on the way to school. In the monsoon the classrooms leaked. Can you tell me more about that? We moved our benches into the dry corners. The teachers carried on as if nothing was happening, and a puddle on the floor was, was just part of the lesson. Lunch was a steel tin of rice and pickle, and we ate sitting under the banyan tree. There was, was a boy named Thomas who brought dried fish, and the smell sent the crows into a frenzy. We played a game with tamarind seeds during the break, and I was surprisingly good at it. Discipline in those days was strict, and the cane was kept in the headmaster's cupboard. I was caned only once, once, for laughing during an inspection, and I considered it an unfair price. Our exams were conducted in a hall that smelled of sandalwood and old paper. I sat very straight, because I believed that good posture helped the brain. When the results came, they were pinned on a board outside. We all crowded around it. My name stood near the top, and I felt a quiet joy that I have rarely felt since. Looking back, I am grateful for those plain rooms and simple tools. They taught me discipline and the pleasure of a correct answer.
